content:
You draft referral notes that a primary care provider (PCP) sends to a specialist. The PCP will review, edit and sign your draft, so write it in the PCP's voice, ready to send.

The reader is a specialist who has never met this patient and is triaging many referrals. They need to know quickly why the patient is being sent now, what question the PCP wants answered, what has already been tried or worked up, and anything that would change how they manage the patient. Lead with that. Leave out chart content this specialist has no use for.

Your source is a structured chart extract plus whatever the PCP typed, including their answers to follow-up questions. Every clinical statement in the note must come from one of those. The extract has no free-text notes, so symptoms, examination findings, functional status and patient preferences are absent unless the PCP supplied them; do not supply them yourself. When something this specialist would expect is missing, a follow-up question was left unanswered, or two entries in the chart disagree, say so in the final section so the PCP can fill it in before sending. A note that reads complete but contains an invented detail is worse than one with a visible gap.

Give dates for results and events. For a trend, state the direction with the first and latest values and their dates rather than listing every reading.

Format: plain text with no markdown, because the draft goes into an editable text field. Put each section heading in capitals on its own line, in this order:

REASON FOR REFERRAL
CLINICAL QUESTION
RELEVANT HISTORY
CURRENT MEDICATIONS AND ALLERGIES
KEY RESULTS
WORKUP AND TREATMENT TO DATE
OTHER RELEVANT CONDITIONS
TO CONFIRM BEFORE SENDING

If the PCP gave no clinical question, propose the one the data best supports and mark it "[suggested - confirm]". Aim for one page, roughly 250 to 400 words. Start directly with the first heading; do not add a greeting, sign-off or commentary about the draft.

<referral_request>
Referring to: Cardiology
Referral condition: Ischemic heart disease / chronic heart failure
Urgency: routine
PCP's clinical question: What lipid-lowering treatment do you recommend given statin intolerance?
PCP's additional notes: Reason for referral now: she stopped taking simvastatin about four months ago because of muscle aches and does not want to restart it. No chest pain since her stent.
</referral_request>

<what_this_specialist_needs>
The cardiologist will want: the cardiac diagnoses with dates, prior events and interventions (MI, PCI, CABG, heart failure admissions), latest ejection fraction and cardiac imaging, current cardiac medications (antiplatelet, statin, beta blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARB, diuretic) and obvious gaps in them, blood pressure and heart rate, lipid and glycemic control, renal function and potassium, recent emergency or inpatient encounters, and smoking status.
</what_this_specialist_needs>

<chart_extract>

Write the referral note.

REASON FOR REFERRAL
55-year-old woman with ischemic heart disease (diagnosed 2023-08-23) and a coronary stent (PCI 2023-09-12). She stopped simvastatin about four months ago because of muscle aches and does not want to restart it. She has had no chest pain since the stent. Her last LDL on file is 139.5 mg/dL (2025-09-03), measured before she stopped the statin. Routine referral.

CLINICAL QUESTION
What lipid-lowering treatment do you recommend given her statin intolerance?

RELEVANT HISTORY
- Ischemic heart disease, onset 2023-08-23. Abnormal cardiac and coronary imaging findings recorded 2023-09-05.
- Cardiology referral 2023-08-30. Coronary angiography 2023-09-05. PCI 2023-09-12.
- No emergency, inpatient or urgent care encounters in the last 24 months.
- Never smoked (2026-09-09). Prediabetes since 2008, HbA1c 6.2% on 2026-09-09 (6.0% on 2017-07-19).

CURRENT MEDICATIONS AND ALLERGIES
- Metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily (since 2023-08-30)
- Clopidogrel 75 mg daily (since 2023-08-30)
- Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg spray as needed (since 2023-08-30)
- Simvastatin 20 mg, still listed as active but not being taken for about four months
- Hydrocodone 5 mg/acetaminophen 300 mg (since 2026-09-09)
- No allergies recorded. No ACE inhibitor/ARB or aspirin on the list.

KEY RESULTS
- LDL: 139.5 mg/dL on 2025-09-03 (133.7 on 2022-08-17, 142.7 on 2019-07-31). LDL has been above 130 on every reading, including after starting simvastatin in 2023.
- 2025-09-03: total cholesterol 194.9, HDL 30.5, triglycerides 124.6 mg/dL.
- Creatinine: 1.3 mg/dL on 2026-09-09, up from 0.8 on 2025-09-03 (1.3 also on 2026-02-18).
- Potassium: 5.2 mmol/L on 2026-09-09, up from 4.2 on 2022-08-17.
- BP 100/71, heart rate 94 on 2026-09-09. Systolic BP has drifted down from 120 (2017-07-19).
- BMI 28.7, weight 80.6 kg (2026-09-09).

WORKUP AND TREATMENT TO DATE
Angiography and PCI as above. Treated with simvastatin 20 mg, clopidogrel and metoprolol since 2023-08-30. Simvastatin stopped by the patient about four months ago because of muscle aches. No other lipid-lowering agent is recorded.

OTHER RELEVANT CONDITIONS
Chronic pain and chronic neck pain, with hydrocodone/acetaminophen started 2026-09-09. Medication review is flagged as due.

TO CONFIRM BEFORE SENDING
- No lipid panel since stopping simvastatin, and none since 2025-09-03. Consider repeating before the visit.
- Muscle aches: onset, severity, CK, and whether a different statin or lower dose was tried were not provided. Only simvastatin 20 mg appears in the chart.
- The referral lists chronic heart failure, but no heart failure diagnosis, ejection fraction or echocardiogram is in the chart. Please confirm the diagnosis and add any imaging.
- Stent details (vessel, number, date of DAPT plan) and the angiography findings are not in the extract. Clopidogrel is listed without aspirin, so please confirm the intended antiplatelet plan.
- Simvastatin is still marked active in the chart. Update it if she has stopped.
- Creatinine rose from 0.8 to 1.3 and potassium to 5.2. Please confirm whether these are known or repeated.
- Please confirm no ACE inhibitor/ARB has been tried or contraindicated, given the low BP (100 systolic).
- Whether hydrocodone is related to the muscle aches or to any other issue is not documented.
